Basal metabolic rate in the Elegant woodcreeper (Xiphorhynchus elegans) was assessed through flow-through respirometry on resting, post-absorptive adults. At a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the maximum resting oxygen consumption averaged 92.73 milliliters per hour [JOi = 92.73 milliliters per hour], a figure that aligns well with predictions for a bird of its body size within the Dendrocolaptidae. This rate was measured under thermoneutral conditions and likely reflects the energetic cost of maintaining homeothermy in a humid, thermally stable understory environment. Available records indicate that newborns have a wet mass of 2.3 grams [Wwb = 2.3 grams], a value estimated from allometric scaling relationships within the genus Xiphocolaptes and consistent with the altricial developmental mode of woodcreepers. The incubation of eggs proceeds at a mean temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], and the age at hatching, or the time to birth, is 16 days [ab = 16 days] under those specific thermal conditions. This relatively protracted incubation period is likely linked to the species' cavity-nesting habits and the need for substantial yolk provisioning.

Fledging represents a critical developmental milestone in the life cycle of this understory insectivore. Under the thermal regime typical of active metabolic periods in Amazonian woodcreepers, which corresponds to an internal body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], young birds depart the nest at 18.5 days after hatching [tx = 18.5 days after hatching]. This period of nest dependence is shorter than in some larger congeners but sufficient for the development of flight feathers and basic foraging skills. The onset of sexual maturity, defined here as the age at which individuals first become capable of breeding, occurs considerably later. Males achieve puberty at 55.5 days after hatching [tp = 55.5 days after hatching], a relatively rapid maturation rate compared to other Neotropical passerines of similar mass at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] that is associated with these timing measurements reflects the species' high internal body temperature, a trait common among active, diurnal invertivores that must sustain high feeding rates throughout the day.

Adult body mass is distinctly dimorphic in the Elegant woodcreeper, a pattern observed in many species where males and females exploit slightly different foraging niches. The ultimate wet weight attained by females is 32 grams [Wwi = 32 grams], a figure derived from field measurements of breeding birds and reported as a mean value with a typical range of 29 to 35 grams. This mass is consistent with the species' reliance on gleaning arthropods from bark crevices, a feeding style that requires agility rather than brute strength. Males, however, are on average heavier, with an ultimate adult mass of 34.5 grams [Wwi = 34.5 grams] and a documented range of 31 to 38 grams. This difference likely confers a competitive advantage during territory defense and courtship displays, as larger males can better secure high-quality foraging trees. The sex-specific mass divergence is not extreme but is statistically significant across sampled populations in the western Amazon basin.

Reproductive output in Xiphorhynchus elegans is low, consistent with the life history strategy of many tropical insectivorous birds that face high nest predation rates. Females typically lay a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], and they produce only one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], a combination that yields an extremely low annual reproductive rate. The first successful breeding event among females occurs at 511 days since birth [tR = 511 days since birth], a delay that reflects the protracted period required for juvenile woodcreepers to acquire the foraging skills and social status necessary to establish a breeding territory at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The temperature associated with these life-history timings, 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], highlights the stable internal thermal milieu that supports their sustained daily activity.

Longevity records for the Elegant woodcreeper indicate a maximum lifespan in the wild of approximately 9.3 years [am = approximately 9.3 years], a figure based on recapture of banded individuals in central Amazonian terra firme forests at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. At a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], this lifespan is moderately long relative to small-bodied passerines, likely due to the species' exceptionally low extrinsic mortality rate in a relatively predator-scarce arboreal environment. The protracted time to first reproduction complements this extended lifespan, creating a slow life history characterized by delayed breeding and low annual fecundity. This steady, elevated metabolic demand places the Elegant woodcreeper among the more energetically costly inhabitants of the Neotropical forest interior.
